title: A faulty kettle: what does the evidence establish?
subtitle: Separate facts, rules and calendar arithmetic.
summary: Compare ten fictional records. Identify a missing fact, distinguish two time limits and explain why a calendar alone cannot decide a dispute.
audience: General readers; no legal vocabulary assumed.
scope: England and Wales; illustrative in-person consumer purchase from a trader. This is a source-reading exercise, not a decision about your dispute or a certified current-law consolidation.

passages.title: A disclosed scratch and a different alleged defect
passages.text: The quality test considers the goods and the circumstances. A condition specifically brought to the buyer’s attention before the contract is treated differently from an undisclosed problem. A disclosed scratch does not, by itself, settle an unrelated allegation about an electrical fault.
passages.context: Original explanation of section 9, especially (2)–(4). The activity stipulates a consumer, a trader and a paid shop sale; it does not determine that status for a real person.

passages.title: One route is not every remedy
passages.text: Section 19 connects nonconformity with different remedies. The six-month provision in subsection (14) names particular routes; it is not a universal shortcut for proving every issue in a short-term rejection. A recording of a malfunction does not by itself establish its cause or its condition at delivery.
passages.context: Original explanation of the selected remedy provisions. Only the fictional record is assessed; no automatic burden-of-proof decision is made.

passages.title: Rejection and a separate refund clock
passages.text: Rejection needs a sufficiently clear indication that the goods are rejected and the contract treated as ended. A question about repair does not necessarily communicate that. The refund provision requires action without undue delay and sets a fourteen-day outer period beginning with the day the trader agrees the consumer is entitled to a refund.
passages.context: Original explanation of section 20(5)–(6), (15). Return arrangements and this refund-agreement clock are distinct from the short-term rejection clock.

passages.title: A conditional thirty-day calendar
passages.text: In the unextended ordinary example, counting begins on the first day after all relevant ownership or possession, delivery and any required installation or enabling-action conditions have occurred. Purchase day alone is insufficient. The section also addresses earlier exercise, perishable goods and repair waiting periods. Those exceptions cannot be resolved by applying the ordinary thirty-day arithmetic indiscriminately.
passages.context: Original explanation of section 22(3)–(8). The calculator uses only stipulated conditions-complete dates. Its dates are examples, not legal-effective dates.

claims.text: The selected rule and a calendar result do not establish all facts needed for a legal conclusion.
claims.qualification: Educational reasoning about stipulated cases; no individual entitlement is decided.

claims.text: The selected provisions use different events to start the rejection and refund clocks.
claims.qualification: Read the cited provision and its qualifications; the two clock calculations are deliberately separate.

context: Consumer and trader are stipulated roles in these examples. Conformity concerns whether the supplied goods meet relevant contract requirements; a remedy is a legal response to an established failure.
A fact stated by the exercise is an assumption, not a document you have independently proved. A missing fact must remain missing.

Source inspection: 23 October 2026. Displayed editorial cutoffs are 22 October for sections 9/20, 20 October for section 19 and 21 October for section 22, with outstanding/future-change notices. No common certified legal snapshot is claimed.
The examples exclude finance, services, digital content, perishables and installation. Repair waiting-period arithmetic is outside this version.
The calendar is computed in whole UTC civil days, avoiding daylight-saving hour differences. An elapsed short-term window does not mean every possible remedy has expired.

cases.title: Last day, with facts stipulated
cases.facts: New domestic kettle from a trader; single paid sale in a shop; s9 nonconformity at delivery stipulated; all trigger conditions complete 1 October; clear rejection communicated 31 October.
cases.feedback: Under the stipulated ordinary conditions, 31 October is day 30. The example assumes a qualifying defect and a clear rejection; the calendar does not prove either.

cases.title: The following day
cases.facts: Same delivery and stipulated defect; communication moved to 1 November; no extension agreement or repair request.
cases.feedback: 1 November is outside the modelled unextended thirty-day period. Other remedies are not assessed and are not declared unavailable.

cases.title: Receipt and delivery are different
cases.facts: Payment receipt 1 October; delivery note 5 October; ownership-transfer date not given.
cases.feedback: The receipt and delivery note do not give the ownership-transfer fact. Do not substitute purchase day for the date all clock conditions were met.

cases.title: A malfunction on video
cases.facts: A video shows malfunction on 10 October; cause and condition at delivery disputed.
cases.feedback: The video supports the described malfunction at that moment. It does not establish its cause or the delivery condition, and this exercise does not assign a legal burden by presumption.

cases.title: A disclosed scratch
cases.facts: A scratch was specifically disclosed before sale; an unrelated electrical fault is alleged.
cases.feedback: Keep the specifically disclosed scratch separate from the alleged electrical fault. The latter still needs evidence; one disclosure is not a blanket answer.

cases.title: A different preferred colour
cases.facts: Kettle functions as described; buyer changes preferred colour after an in-person sale.
cases.feedback: Changing a colour preference is not the stipulated quality defect. A voluntary returns policy or a different type of contract would need its own facts.

cases.title: An inquiry about repair
cases.facts: Buyer asks whether the shop can repair the kettle; no clear rejection statement is stipulated.
cases.feedback: The wording does not establish a clear rejection. An actual repair request can also affect the clock; do not infer both from mere contact.

cases.title: Agreement to refund
cases.facts: Trader agrees to refund on 31 October; return collection is discussed separately.
cases.feedback: 31 October is day one of the separate illustrative refund period, giving 13 November as its outer date. The duty to act without undue delay remains relevant.

cases.title: Before delivery
cases.facts: Goods have not yet been delivered; a clear rejection is proposed.
cases.feedback: No completed clock-trigger date is supplied. A counting window that has not started is not automatically a bar to exercising a right earlier; other conditions still matter.

cases.title: A repair waiting period
cases.facts: Repair agreed; returned item may still be nonconforming.
cases.feedback: This version does not model repair waiting periods or returned-goods conditions. It deliberately returns no ordinary deadline for this case.

activity.transfer: A receipt is dated 1 March, delivery is dated 5 March, and ownership transfer is unstated. Name the missing fact before attempting the ordinary calendar. Then explain why an unrelated disclosed scratch would not settle a different alleged defect.
rubric: Separate the date of purchase from all required clock-trigger conditions.
Identify the exact proposition each document supports; do not infer delivery condition from later malfunction alone.
Keep rejection, refund agreement and any repair waiting period separate.
State which route is outside the model without declaring every remedy unavailable.
